beats.narration_text: Aloha. This is Liam, in for Bear, with chapter thirteen of INFO 7375, Computational Skepticism for AI, at Northeastern. This film is about why more data can't make a model safe everywhere. Data covers a region of the world, and every region has an edge. You'll watch the sample grow and the edge move, and never vanish. The trap: treating the gap as an amount that shrinks.

props.heading: What This Film Is About
props.question: If more data makes a model better, why can't enough data make it safe?
lines: Data covers a region of the world, and every region has an edge.
You will watch the sample grow and the edge move — and never vanish.
The trap: treating the gap as an amount that shrinks. It is a place: past the edge.

beats.narration_text: Why should you care? Every validation number you report was measured inside the sample's edge. Read ninety-nine point seven percent as a fact about the world, and you'll miss the case that matters. Know where the edge is, and you know which cases need a human. That is the supervisor's job, and no amount of scaling does it for you.

beats.narration_text: Three terms. A sample: the cases a model learned from, a part of the world, never all of it. In-distribution: a new case that looks like the cases in the sample. And distribution shift: when the cases a system meets stop looking like its sample.

a new case that looks like the cases in the sample
when the cases a system meets stop looking like its sample

learn.question: The turkey's evidence was never wrong for a thousand days. Why did it fail?
learn.action: Ride the confidence curve day by day to 1,000, then mark day 1,001.
learn.observation: Confidence rises every day and peaks on the last safe morning.
learn.inference: More days made the turkey more confident, not safer.
learn.next_question: Would more data have saved it? What does 'more data' do to a sample?

beats.narration_text: A turkey is fed every morning for a thousand days. Each morning is evidence that the human cares about it, and its confidence climbs. It never once dips. Day one thousand is the most confident it has ever been. Day one thousand and one is Thanksgiving. So here's the puzzle: would more days of data have saved it?

shot.visual_intent: Left: axes 'day 0 · 500 · 1,000' and 'confidence' (no scale); an ink dot rides a monotonically rising curve from day 0 to 1,000. A dashed 'day 1,001' line appears just past the axis with a terracotta dot. Right: the puzzle — 'Would more days of data have saved it?' — and three short facts.

show.event: axes draw; the dot starts riding the curve

shot.motion_claim: The key case, unsolved: confidence highest on the last safe day.

learn.question: What does a validation number cover?
learn.action: Draw the tested cases as a region inside the region of everything deployment could bring.
learn.observation: The sample is a region; the world is bigger; the sample has an edge.
learn.inference: 99.7% is a fact about the inside of that region.
learn.next_question: What happens to the edge when we add data?

beats.narration_text: Now a system instead of a turkey. It's tested on ten thousand routine cases, and it gets ninety-nine point seven percent of them right. Draw those cases as a region: that's the sample. Draw everything the system could meet once it's deployed as a bigger region around it: that's the world. And notice: the sample has an edge.

shot.visual_intent: The turkey panel clears. Left: '10,000 routine cases', '99.7% right'. Right: the WORLD (dim outline, 'the world') draws; the SAMPLE — an ink-edged region with dim case-dots — grows inside it; 'sample' labels it; a terracotta dot sits on its edge.
shot.motion_claim: First instance: a real validation number drawn as a region with an edge.

learn.question: What does more data do?
learn.observation: The uncovered part shrinks; the edge moves out and is still there.
learn.next_question: Keep going — does the gap shrink to nothing?

beats.narration_text: Add more data. The sample grows, and its edge moves out. Add more again. It moves out again. Each time, the part of the world the data never reached gets smaller. And each time, look where the edge is: still there, just further out.

shot.visual_intent: The sample grows twice (more case-dots each time); the edge travels outward. Left: a bar per enlargement for 'not yet reached' — three ink bars, each shorter. A terracotta dot rides the new edge.

show.event: enlargement 2: edge moves out again; bar 3
dot on the edge: still there

shot.motion_claim: Second instance, one parameter varied (sample size), shown moving: the edge persists.

learn.question: If the uncovered part keeps shrinking, doesn't the limit vanish?
learn.action: Extrapolate the shrinking bars to zero; then measure the turkey's gap the same way.
learn.observation: The turkey's gap was under a tenth of a percent and it was the whole story.
learn.inference: The size of the uncovered part is the wrong measurement.
learn.next_question: If not how much, then what?

beats.narration_text: Here's the obvious conclusion, and a serious critic makes it. The gap is shrinking. Keep scaling, and it shrinks to nothing, so the limit is only a frequency. But the turkey's gap was one morning in a thousand and one: under a tenth of a percent. Tiny, and it was the only morning that mattered. Measuring how much is uncovered was the wrong measurement.

shot.visual_intent: Left: the critic's line — 'scale it enough, and / the gap shrinks to nothing?' — and a dim dashed extrapolation through the three bar tops down to zero at 'enough'. Then 'turkey: 1 morning in 1,001' and 'under 0.1% — and it mattered'; a terracotta X beside the extrapolation's zero.

show.event: the dashed trend runs to zero

shot.motion_claim: The natural wrong turn — the functionalist's frequency argument — walked to where it breaks.

learn.question: Where is the gap, if not an amount?
learn.action: Label the excluded ring and grow the sample once more.
learn.observation: Sample and excluded trade exactly; the edge travels with both.
learn.inference: The edge is defined by where the data stopped; the gap lives there.
learn.next_question: Where would the turkey's day 1,001 sit in this picture?

beats.narration_text: So stop measuring how much. Look at where. The sample is everything the data reached. The excluded part is everything it didn't. Grow one, and the other shrinks by exactly that much: they're complementary, two sides of one line. And that line, the edge, is defined by where the data stopped. The gap doesn't live in the middle. It lives at the edge.

shot.visual_intent: Left: three rows — 'sample: what the data reached', 'excluded: what it did not', 'edge: where the data stopped' — then bold 'the gap lives at the edge'. Right: 'excluded' labels the ring; the sample grows once more while the ring shrinks; a terracotta dot rides the edge.

show.event: grow: the ring shrinks by what the sample gained

shot.motion_claim: The representation: sample and excluded region as complements; the edge is the object.

learn.question: Where does day 1,001 land among the turkey's mornings?
learn.action: Hold the picture; name the move.
learn.observation: The viewer commits: inside or outside, and whether more mornings help.
learn.inference: A prediction makes the move evidence.

beats.narration_text: Before it moves, commit. Put the turkey's thousand mornings into this picture: every fed morning is a case in its sample. Where does day one thousand and one land, inside or outside? And if we added more fed mornings, would that move it in?

shot.visual_intent: The turkey curve returns left with its day-1,001 marker (terracotta dot); the right panel holds the world with the generic sample ghosted; an ink pointer runs from the curve to the world; 'inside or outside?' lands; everything holds.

show.event: turkey curve back; the generic sample ghosts
pointer: the mornings are going in

learn.question: Do more fed mornings move day 1,001 inside?
learn.action: Pour the curve's mornings into the world; stretch the sample with more of them.
learn.observation: The edge moves along the routine; the event stays outside.
learn.inference: A sample of fed mornings cannot contain the morning that was not a feeding — the exclusion is what made it a sample.

beats.narration_text: Watch. Every fed morning lands inside. The last one is the edge. Day one thousand and one lands outside. Now add more fed mornings. The edge moves, along the routine. The event doesn't come in. More mornings like these can't contain the morning that wasn't one.

shot.visual_intent: The turkey curve's day-dots fly into the world panel and settle into a long, flat sample — 'fed mornings' — wrapped by an ink edge; the terracotta day-1,001 dot flies to a spot above it, outside. Then the sample stretches along the routine (more dots at both ends): the edge moves; the event stays out. 'more fed mornings' · 'still outside'.

show.event: the mornings fly in; the edge wraps them
more fed mornings: the sample stretches

shot.motion_claim: The aha: the turkey's curve IS a sample with an edge; enlarging it along the routine never reaches the event.

learn.question: What is the rule?
learn.action: Name the gap; state it in the chapter's words beside the picture.
learn.observation: Sample and excluded are complements; the edge is defined by the exclusion.
learn.inference: No enlargement crosses a boundary defined by what the enlargement did not reach.
learn.next_question: Does the same shape explain a real validation?

beats.narration_text: This thing we keep pointing at deserves its name: the data-world gap. The parts of the world not in the data are not learnable from the data. Not because the data is small, but because the sample and what it excluded are complementary by construction. Scaling moves the edge. It never removes it. David Hume made the underlying point in seventeen forty-eight: you can't justify expecting the unseen to resemble the seen by pointing at the seen.

shot.visual_intent: Left: 'the data-world gap' lands bold with a terracotta dot beside it; under it 'not in the data →' / 'not learnable from the data'; then 'scaling moves the edge; it never removes it'; then dim 'after Hume (1748), Enquiry §IV'. Right: the turkey world holds with 'sample' and 'excluded' labels; the edge is retraced.
shot.motion_claim: The abstraction arrives as the name for what was watched.

learn.question: Does the edge explain a validated system that harmed people?
learn.action: Put the 94% inside the sample and the three harms outside it.
learn.observation: The accuracy and the harms sit on opposite sides of the edge.
learn.inference: Accuracy is a fact about the inside; the edge is where the supervisor must look.
learn.next_question: Back to the turkey: would more data have saved it?

beats.narration_text: Same shape, higher stakes. The chapter opens on a composite case, not a single incident: a clinical system at ninety-four percent accuracy, every threshold met, and within six months of going live, three patients harmed. The ninety-four percent was real, over the question the data could answer. The three patients were in a region the data could not reach. In distribution, accuracy holds. At the edge, it says nothing.

shot.visual_intent: Right: the turkey sample morphs into a clinic's sample with '94%' inside; three ink dots appear outside the edge; '3 harmed' with a terracotta dot beside. Left: 'tested: does this match the data?' / 'harmed: what is going on with this patient?'. Caption: 'a composite, not one incident'.

show.event: three dots outside the edge; '3 harmed'

shot.motion_claim: Post-shift instance: a real validation number read on the new representation.

learn.question: Would more days of data have saved the turkey?
learn.action: Return to the curve and the day-1,001 marker with the sample picture beside it.
learn.observation: More mornings raise the curve and move the edge, never across.
learn.inference: The saving question is whether a case is inside the edge — the supervisor's check.

beats.narration_text: Back to the turkey. Would more days of data have saved it? More fed mornings raise the curve and move the edge. They never carry it across. Its confidence peaked on the last safe day, because confidence is measured inside the edge. The question that saves it isn't how much data. It's whether tomorrow is inside. Watching for that shift, and overriding when a case lands outside, is the supervisor's job. Not taught here: meaning and intentionality, which ride on this same gap.

shot.visual_intent: The HOOK's turkey curve returns left with the day-1,001 marker; right: the turkey's sample and the event outside. 'more data: the edge moves' and 'never across' land; 'is tomorrow inside?' lands bold; a terracotta dot on the event; dim caption 'not taught here: meaning, intent'.

show.event: the HOOK's curve and the turkey world
sample stretches once more; the event stays out

shot.motion_claim: The HOOK's curve resolved: the question is location, not quantity.

beats.narration_text: Let's recap with Claude. Data covers a region of the world: the sample. Every sample has an edge. More data moves the edge outward. It never removes it, because the sample and what it excluded are complementary by construction. What the data excluded isn't learnable from the data. So accuracy is a fact about inside the edge, and whether a case is inside is the supervisor's call.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude: Two systems each score 99.7% on ten thousand routine test cases. One predicts how long employees take to walk to work. The other predicts the losses on financial returns. Before explaining anything, predict for each: are the cases it has not seen drawn from Mediocristan, where outliers do not dominate, or Extremistan, where one case can outweigh all the rest? Then describe each sample and its edge, and name one case that would sit past that edge. Finally, explain why adding more routine cases cannot move that case inside. Two things to look for. Did it predict before it explained? If it jumped to the answer, send it back. And in the last part, does it argue from where the edge is, or does it just say the model needs more data?
